test_text.title: Why being bored is stimulating - and useful, too

article.title: Why being bored is stimulating - and useful, too

items.sentence_raw: We all know how it feels - it's impossible to keep your mind on anything, time stretches out, and all the things you could do seem equally unlikely to make you feel better.
But defining boredom so that it can be studied in the lab has proved difficult.
items.explain: Q14: The passage says *'defining boredom so that it can be studied in the lab has proved difficult'* — this shows a **problem** with the **scientific approach**. The heading **iv** (*'Problems with a scientific approach to boredom'*) matches this exactly. So the answer is **iv**.

items.sentence_raw: For a start, it can include a lot of other mental states, such as frustration, apathy, depression and indifference.
There isn't even agreement over whether boredom is always a low-energy, flat kind of emotion or whether feeling agitated and restless counts as boredom, too.
In his book, Boredom: A Lively History, Peter Toohey at the University of Calgary, Canada, compares it to disgust - an emotion that motivates us to stay away from certain situations.
"If disgust protects humans from infection, boredom may protect them from 'infectious' social situations," he suggests.
items.explain: Q20: The passage says boredom *'may protect them from 'infectious' social situations'* — **'protect from'** means **'avoid an unpleasant experience'**. This matches idea **E** (*'Boredom may encourage us to avoid an unpleasant experience'*). So the answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: By asking people about their experiences of boredom, Thomas Goetz and his team at the University of Konstanz in Germany have recently identified five distinct types: indifferent, calibrating, searching, reactant and apathetic.
items.explain: Q15: The passage says Goetz *'identified five distinct types'* of boredom — this is a **system of classification**. The heading **vi** (*'Creating a system of classification for feelings of boredom'*) matches this. So the answer is **vi**.

items.sentence_raw: These can be plotted on two axes - one running left to right, which measures low to high arousal, and the other from top to bottom, which measures how positive or negative the feeling is.
Intriguingly, Goetz has found that while people experience all kinds of boredom, they tend to specialise in one.
Of the five types, the most damaging is 'reactant' boredom with its explosive combination of high arousal and negative emotion.
items.explain: Q21: The passage says *'the most damaging is 'reactant' boredom'* — **'most damaging'** means **'worse than all the others'**. This matches idea **B** (*'One sort of boredom is worse than all the others'*). So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: The most useful is what Goetz calls 'indifferent' boredom: someone isn't engaged in anything satisfying but still feels relaxed and calm.
However, it remains to be seen whether there are any character traits that predict the kind of boredom each of us might be prone to.
Psychologist Sandi Mann at the University of Central Lancashire, UK, goes further.
"All emotions are there for a reason, including boredom," she says.
Mann has found that being bored makes us more creative.
items.explain: Q16: The passage says *'being bored makes us more creative'* — **'creative'** means producing new ideas, which is a **productive outcome**. The heading **i** (*'The productive outcomes that may result from boredom'*) matches this. So the answer is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: "We're all afraid of being bored but in actual fact it can lead to all kinds of amazing things," she says.

In experiments published last year, Mann found that people who had been made to feel bored by copying numbers out of the phone book for 15 minutes came up with more creative ideas about how to use a polystyrene cup than a control group.
Mann concluded that a passive, boring activity is best for creativity because it allows the mind to wander.
In fact, she goes so far as to suggest that we should seek out more boredom in our lives.
Psychologist John Eastwood at York University in Toronto, Canada, isn't convinced.
"If you are in a state of mind-wandering you are not bored," he says.
"In my view, by definition boredom is an undesirable state."
That doesn't necessarily mean that it isn't adaptive, he adds.
"Pain is adaptive - if we didn't have physical pain, bad things would happen to us.
Does that mean that we should actively cause pain?
No.
But even if boredom has evolved to help us survive, it can still be toxic if allowed to fester."
For Eastwood, the central feature of boredom is a failure to put our 'attention system' into gear.
This causes an inability to focus on anything, which makes time seem to go painfully slowly.
items.explain: Q24: The passage says boredom causes *'an inability to focus on anything'* — **'inability to focus'** means people **cannot focus**. So the answer is **focus**.

items.sentence_raw: What's more, your efforts to improve the situation can end up making you feel worse.
items.explain: Q22: The passage says *'your efforts to improve the situation can end up making you feel worse'* — **'efforts to improve'** means **'trying to cope'**, and **'making you feel worse'** means **'increase its negative effects'**. This matches idea **D** (*'Trying to cope with boredom can increase its negative effects'*). So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: "People try to connect with the world and if they are not successful there's that frustration and irritability," he says.
Perhaps most worryingly, says Eastwood, repeatedly failing to engage attention can lead to a state where we don't know what to do any more, and no longer care.
Eastwood's team is now trying to explore why the attention system fails.
It's early days
but they think that at least some of it comes down to personality.
Boredom proneness has been linked with a variety of traits.
People who are motivated by pleasure seem to suffer particularly badly.
items.explain: Q25: The passage says *'People who are motivated by pleasure seem to suffer particularly badly'* — **'motivated by pleasure'** means **pleasure** is an important aim. So the answer is **pleasure**.

items.sentence_raw: Other personality traits, such as curiosity, are associated with a high boredom threshold.
items.explain: Q26: The passage says *'personality traits, such as curiosity, are associated with a high boredom threshold'* — a **'high boredom threshold'** means you can **cope with it**. So the answer is **curiosity**.

items.sentence_raw: More evidence that boredom has detrimental effects comes from studies of people who are more or less prone to boredom.
It seems those who bore easily face poorer prospects in education, their career and even life in general.
items.explain: Q18: The passage says *'those who bore easily face poorer prospects'* — this means we can **identify** people who are **most affected** by boredom. The heading **viii** (*'Identifying those most affected by boredom'*) matches this. So the answer is **viii**.

items.sentence_raw: But of course, boredom itself cannot kill - it's the things we do to deal with it that may put us in danger.
items.explain: Q17: The passage says *'the things we do to deal with it may put us in danger'* — this is a **potential danger** from how we react to boredom. The heading **v** (*'A potential danger arising from boredom'*) matches this. So the answer is **v**.

items.sentence_raw: What can we do to alleviate it before it comes to that?
Goetz's group has one suggestion.

Working with teenagers, they found that those who 'approach' a boring situation - in other words, see that it's boring and get stuck in anyway - report less boredom than those who try to avoid it by using snacks, TV or social media for distraction.
Psychologist Francoise Wemelsfelder speculates that our over-connected lifestyles might even be a new source of boredom.
items.explain:
Q19: The passage says our *'over-connected lifestyles'* are a *'new source of boredom'* — this is a **new explanation**. It also says we should *'use boredom to motivate us'* — this is a **new cure**. The heading **iii** (*'A new explanation and a new cure for boredom'*) matches both. So the answer is **iii**.

Q23: The passage says our *'over-connected lifestyles might even be a new source of boredom'* — **'over-connected lifestyles'** means **'the way we live today'**. This matches idea **A** (*'The way we live today may encourage boredom'*). So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: "In modern human society there is a lot of overstimulation but still a lot of problems finding meaning," she says.
So instead of seeking yet more mental stimulation, perhaps we should leave our phones alone, and use boredom to motivate us to engage with the world in a more meaningful way.
items.explain: Q19: The passage says our *'over-connected lifestyles'* are a *'new source of boredom'* — this is a **new explanation**. It also says we should *'use boredom to motivate us'* — this is a **new cure**. The heading **iii** (*'A new explanation and a new cure for boredom'*) matches both. So the answer is **iii**.

subtitles: This most common of emotions is turning out to be more interesting than we thought
